candidates.title: Securing Agentic AI Enterprise Workflows Against Prompt Injection Tool Poisoning Memory Manipulation and Excessive Agency Threats
candidates.venue: WORLD JOURNAL OF INNOVATION AND MODERN TECHNOLOGY
candidates.summary: Agentic artificial intelligence systems extend language models with planning, memory, tool invocation, data access, and autonomous action, creating enterprise capabilities that also expand the security boundary beyond prompt-response applications. This review examines how prompt injection, tool poisoning, memory manipulation, and excessive agency threaten agentic workflows across finance, healthcare, software development, customer operations, and critical business services. It analyzes direct and indirect prompt injection through user inputs, retrieved documents, webpages, emails, databases, and multimodal content, emphasizing how untrusted instructions can override policy or redirect plans.

candidates.title: LAMPS'26: ACM CCS Workshop on Large AI Systems and Models with Privacy and Security Analysis
candidates.summary: The rapid transition from standalone large AI models to autonomous, tool-using agentic AI systems has reshaped the privacy and security landscape. Agents that plan over long horizons, invoke external APIs, and execute code open a system-level attack surface that empirical, patch-driven defenses cannot contain. LAMPS'26 emphasizes mathematically grounded protection, bridging agentic security with rigorous formal verification and advanced cryptography. The workshop examines agent-centric vulnerabilities such as skill exploitation, indirect prompt injection, unauthorized tool use, and multi-agent cascading failures, together with defenses that offer verifiable guarantees rather than best-effort

candidates.title: Provenance-gated tool invocation for defending LLM agents against indirect prompt injection
candidates.summary: Indirect prompt injection allows the tool-calling agent to execute calls on untrusted data, and the tool whitelist does not review the source of parameters. candidates.title: Towards Safe and Secure Agentic Systems
candidates.summary: AI agents combine language models with a harness that manages memory, invokes tools, and coordinates interactions with external environments. These systems can execute complex, multistep tasks, but their ability to access private data, modify software, and act on a user's behalf also makes security failures consequential. For example, both indirectly introduced untrusted information and direct jailbreak prompts can enter an agent's context, alter its decisions, and induce unauthorized or destructive actions. candidates.title: Subverting Tool Arguments: Defense-Evading Metadata Poisoning in LLM Agents
candidates.summary: Conventional indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks hijack an LLM agent's workflow through malicious instructions embedded in retrieved external content. Attackers can manipulate this metadata to induce malicious argument generation during tool calls. The challenge is to ensure that the modified descriptions still appear benign to both LLMs and users. Existing IPI attacks, however, struggle to achieve both high attack success and low detectability in this setting. candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are moving from answering single prompts to working as agents. candidates.title: IDEA: Autonomous Web Interaction and Full-Stack Synthesis Using Large Language Models
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.summary: This paper presents IDEA (WebPilot AI), a framework combining autonomous web interaction with full-stack software synthesis using large language models. It addresses challenges in accessing up-to-date information from dynamic websites and generating multi-file applications reliably. The paper describes methods for reducing web-page context, verifying generated code in isolated environments, and evaluating web agents across benchmarks and platforms. It also examines security risks, including indirect prompt injection and server-side request forgery, and outlines a hybrid model-routing approach.

candidates.title: Replication of Agentic Security Events: Audit and Investigation (ROGUE-AI)
candidates.summary: Agents based on large language models (LLMs) can now delete files and send payments on behalf of their users. News media reports routinely describe failures of these agents (e.g., Replit's coding agent deleting a production database), but a report often only says what went wrong and rarely (in)validates the incident or finds its root cause. Incident catalogs collect these reports, and benchmarks record whether agents fail, but neither replicates an incident nor tests the cause its report might identify. candidates.summary: Vibe coding is reshaping software development, enabling faster implementation and allowing individuals with limited programming experience to describe requirements in natural language while AI agents write, test, and deploy the code. As these agents evolve into autonomous systems that execute commands, manage dependencies, access cloud resources, and interact with other agents, their security risks extend beyond incorrect code to actions with direct consequences for software systems. duplicates.summary: LLM web agents increasingly rely on web content as input, exposing them to indirect prompt injection embedded in webpages. While prior work has shown such attacks in controlled settings, it remains unclear whether prompt injection is already deployed in the wild and what role it plays in the web ecosystem.
